title: Lower the gaze
hookLine: believing men and women are both told to lower their gaze and guard their modesty (24:30–31)

lines: APPS BUILT TO HOLD YOUR EYES.
cards: A face across the train car. A stranger's phone screen, lit up and readable. A photo that stops the thumb mid-scroll.

The eyes move first, before anyone has decided anything, and then they linger. Advertisers know this, and so does every app built to keep a thumb scrolling. Surah An-Nur gives a short instruction about the eyes.
It is often remembered as a rule for women alone. Look at who hears it first.

teach.b: Verse thirty. Pickthall: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." Men first.
Then the next verse turns to women with the same opening: "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and be modest". Same verbs, same duty.
The verse to women goes on with more detail about dress, and scholars have written a great deal about that. But the gaze comes first, and it's shared. The Arabic is yaghuddu min absarihim.
Ghadd means to lower, to lessen, the way you'd lower your voice. And the little word min, from, matters. Some commentators read it as: lower some of your gaze.
Not shut your eyes, not walk around staring at your shoes. You still see the person you're talking to. What gets lowered is the lingering, the second look that turns into staring.
A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the same point. The Prophet ﷺ told 'Ali: don't follow one glance with another.
The first is yours; the second is not. The first look just happens. The second is a choice.
And it isn't only about attraction.

In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet listed the rights of the road for people who sit by the street, and lowering the gaze is the first of them. Next to it: not harming anyone, returning greetings, encouraging good.
So guarding the eyes is also manners: not staring into the neighbor's open door, not reading a stranger's messages over their shoulder, not lingering on someone who'd rather not be looked at.

how: Many Muslims understand lowering the gaze as avoiding lingering or immodest looks, for men and women alike, and some extend it to what they choose to watch online.

o: lowering the gaze, letting the second look go
closing the eyes fully during prayer
avoiding all eye contact with other people

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an tells only women to lower their gaze
24:30 tells the believing men first; 24:31 tells the women the same.
lowering the gaze means walking with your eyes on the ground
some commentators read min as 'some of': lower the lingering, not your sight.
a hadith says the first glance is not held against you
the Prophet told 'Ali: the first is yours, the second is not.

games.q: you're sitting on a bench by the street, as people did in Medina. the Prophet lists the rights of the road. what comes first?
games.why: lowering the gaze comes first in Bukhari's report, then not causing harm, returning greetings and encouraging good.

practice: Lower your gaze gently toward the floor in front of you, not closed, just softened, and notice how often your eyes want to move. Each time they do, let them come back. Keep the first look, and let the second one go.

wordCard.voice: Ghadd al-basar. Lowering the gaze: keep the first look, let go of the second. Said first to men, then to women.

orig.note: Arabic: lowering the gaze; ghadd is to lower or lessen, basar is sight.

carryVoice: Your line: guard the eyes. The first look happens; the second is a choice. That's day four hundred ninety-four.
